features.claim: Diplodocus was a very large, long-necked, four-legged animal with a long, whip-like tail.
features.quote: Among the best-known sauropods, Diplodocus were very large, long-necked, quadrupedal animals, with long, whip-like tails.

features.claim: Its front limbs were a little shorter than its back limbs, so its body was mostly horizontal.
features.quote: Their forelimbs were slightly shorter than their hind limbs, resulting in a largely horizontal posture.
It had a short 6 ft long head.

features.claim: Its teeth were small and peg-like, pointed forward, and only at the front of the jaws.
features.quote: Diplodocus had small, 'peg'-like teeth that pointed forward and were only present in the anterior sections of the jaws.

features.claim: Its teeth were in rows like a comb.
features.quote:
Teeth:
in rows like a comb

features.claim: Its tail was about 55% of its total body length.
features.quote: The estimated tail length of Diplodocus makes up approximately 55% of the total body length, with the tail sometimes hypothesized to be capable of functioning like a very long, tapering bullwhip.

features.claim: It had no claws on all but one digit of the front limb, and that claw was unusually large, flattened from side to side, and detached from the bones of the hand.
features.quote: Diplodocus lacked claws on all but one digit of the front limb, and this claw was unusually large relative to other sauropods, flattened from side to side, and detached from the bones of the hand.

features.claim: Some species had narrow, pointed, keratinous spines, much like those on an iguana, up to 18 centimeters long on the whiplash part of their tails.
features.quote: The discovery of partial diplodocid skin impressions in 1990 showed that some species had narrow, pointed, keratinous spines, much like those on an iguana.

not_this.claim: Older pictures showed Diplodocus with its legs sprawled out like a lizard, but this was shown to be wrong.
not_this.quote: This hypothesis was contested by William Jacob Holland, who demonstrated that a sprawling Diplodocus would have needed a trench through which to pull its belly.

not_this.claim: Older pictures showed Diplodocus with its neck held high up in the air, but studies concluded its neutral neck posture was close to horizontal.
not_this.quote: Studies looking at the morphology of sauropod necks have concluded that the neutral posture of Diplodocus neck was close to horizontal, rather than vertical, and scientists such as Kent Stevens have used this to argue that sauropods including Diplodocus did not raise their heads much above shoulder level.

debated.claim: Scientists debate how Diplodocus held its long neck.
debated.quote: There’s been some debate over how it would have held such a long neck.

debated.claim: The flexibility of the Diplodocus neck is debated.
debated.quote: The flexibility of Diplodocus neck is debated but it should have been able to browse from low levels to about 4 metres (13 feet) when on all fours.

second_reading.claim: Its neck was made of at least 15 vertebrae.
second_reading.quote: Its braincase was small, and the neck was composed of at least 15 vertebrae.
second_reading.why: a picture could not show it

second_reading.claim: Its tail was made of about 80 caudal vertebrae.
second_reading.quote: This extremely long tail is composed of about 80 caudal vertebrae, which are almost double the number some of the earlier sauropods had in their tails (such as Shunosaurus with 43), and far more than contemporaneous macronarians had (such as Camarasaurus with 53).
second_reading.why: a picture could not show it

second_reading.claim: The middle of its tail had double beams, which are oddly shaped chevron bones on the underside.
second_reading.quote: The middle part of the tail had "double beams" (oddly shaped chevron bones on the underside, which gave Diplodocus its name).
second_reading.why: a picture could not show it

second_reading.claim: Its front feet had finger and hand bones arranged into a vertical column, horseshoe-shaped in cross section.
second_reading.quote: Like other sauropods, the manus (front "feet") of Diplodocus were highly modified, with the finger and hand bones arranged into a vertical column, horseshoe-shaped in cross section.
second_reading.why: a picture could not show it

second_reading.claim: A documentary showed a mother Diplodocus using an ovipositor to lay eggs, but that was pure speculation.
second_reading.quote: The documentary Walking with Dinosaurs portrayed a mother Diplodocus using an ovipositor to lay eggs, but it was pure speculation on the part of the documentary author.
second_reading.why: a picture could not show it

second_reading.claim: No skull has ever been found that can be confidently said to belong to Diplodocus.
second_reading.quote: No skull has ever been found that can be confidently said to belong to Diplodocus, though skulls of other diplodocids closely related to Diplodocus (such as Galeamopus) are well known.
second_reading.why: a picture could not show it

second_reading.claim: The function of the unusually specialized claw on the front limb is unknown.
second_reading.quote: The function of this unusually specialized claw is unknown.
second_reading.why: a picture could not show it
